s0: We've looked at GPFS, which spreads its intelligence across every node, and Luster, which separates metadata from data and gives each disk a single owner. Now the third of the big three, BGFS, whose makers describe it as built for performance and ease of use. Its design fits on a postcard, four kinds of service, a management service that keeps a registry, metadata servers that know where things are, storage servers that hold the data, and a client that mounts it all as an ordinary directory. Watch a file open. The client asks a metadata server about the file, learns how it's striped, and then streams data to and from the storage servers directly in parallel. We'll cover where it came from, how files are striped and how metadata is spread out, what it promises about consistency, the network layer, mirroring, a burst buffer tool called Beyond, and how it compares with the other two. And I'll flag the places where I couldn't verify a claim.
s1: BGFS began in 2005 as an in-house project at the Fraunhofer Institute for Industrial Mathematics in Germany to replace the file system on the Institute's new compute cluster. Its original name was FHGFS for Fraunhofer-Gesselshaft file system. The first beta was announced at ISCO7 in Dresden and shown at SCO7 in Reno. The first stable major release followed about a year later. In 2014, a spin-off company, Think Park Q, was founded to maintain it and sell support, and the software was renamed BGFS. Development continues in cooperation with Fraunhofer. By then, about 100 customers used it with commercial support. Among them universities, research labs and companies in finance and oil and gas. One difference from the other two stories. I could not find a single founding paper for BGFS comparable to the 2002 papers for GPFS and Luster. The documentation is the primary source here, alongside trade press interviews which are mostly vendor voices. I'll say which is which. Licensing is different too. The client is GPL version 2. The servers are proprietary but a community edition is free to use, and the enterprise edition adds features and requires a support subscription. We'll see exactly which features in a few minutes because it matters.
s2: Start with what BGFS is built on. The servers are ordinary user space programs, not kernel modules, running on top of a local file system on each target. Metadata usually sits on X4 and storage usually on XFS, according to the documentation and a partner's guide. The client is the only piece in the kernel, a patchless module that's compiled for your running kernel, with no reboot needed to install or update it. Any combination of services can share a machine, and you can run several instances on one. The company's line is that you can start with two servers and add components on the fly. That's a vendor claim, though it matches the design. Compare the philosophies. GPSS brings its own software raid and a token-based lock manager. Lustre brings a distributed lock manager and its own network layer. BGFS leans on the local file system, and on whatever raid or ZFS you put underneath. A partner company called it the most lightweight of the three, which is also a vendor-side opinion. Thin has a price, and we'll find it. Fewer documented guarantees and some protection features sitting in the paid edition.
s3: The Management Service is the registry and the watchdog. It keeps a list of every other service and its state. It stores no user data, isn't in the I-O path, and isn't performance critical. One vendor measured its entire database at 88 kilobytes. Metadata services store the namespace, directory information, ownership and permissions, and the stripe pattern of each file. Each instance has exactly one metadata target, a local file system, typically X4 on mirrored flash. Storage services hold the file contents as chunk files. A storage target is typically a hardware RAID 6, 8 plus 2 or 10 plus 2, or ZFS RAID Z2. Adding storage servers adds both capacity and bandwidth. The client mounts the file system by default at slash mnt slash beaks and asks the management service for the topology. From then on it talks straight to the metadata and storage servers. Once a file is open, the metadata server takes no part in reads or writes until it's closed. Here's an open. The client asks the metadata server gets the stripe pattern, then sends I-O in parallel to the storage servers. It's the same shape as luster. The differences are in what each piece does, and that's the next few scenes. There's also an optional monitoring service that feeds a time series database for dashboards. An older documentation describes an optional admin GUI service. Neither is on the data path.
s4: Files are striped across storage targets in chunks. One documentation page gives the default chunk size as 512 kilobytes, though an example output elsewhere in the same doc shows one megabyte, so check your own installation. The simplest pattern, called RAID 0, is plain striping. Chunk 1 to the first target, chunk 2 to the second, and so on around. Each target stores a file's share as a chunk file, one per file per target. Chunk files are created only when something is written, and they aren't preallocated. A 1-byte write makes a 1-byte chunk file. You set the pattern per directory, how many targets, and what chunk size. In version 8, the command is beaks entry set. New files inherit the pattern. Existing files don't change. To restrict them, you recreate them, or migrate them. How are targets chosen? By default, randomly. Targets are also labeled normal, low, or emergency, according to free space, and the chooser prefers normal ones. The thresholds are set on the management service, and I couldn't find their default values. Random choice should sound like the balance problem from the Luster video. So here is my toy model again. 100 targets, thousands of files with a heavy tail of sizes, 4 stripes each, and no free space steering. The fullest target ends up about 1.9 times the average. The capacity labels exist to push back against exactly that. One practical tip from the docks. Keep a chunk within the client's RDM of buffer size, so messages aren't split, and a chunk size of a few megabytes can cut the message count and improve performance, even on a single target.
s5: Now the part BGFS does differently from Luster. Metadata is distributed per directory. Each metadata server owns an exclusive part of the namespace. And when a directory is created, it's assigned to a metadata server by default at random. The docs say each directory's contents live on one metadata node. So a tree of directories fans out across all the metadata servers from the start, with no extra feature to switch on, unlike Luster's DNE. And the documentation says more metadata servers can be added later. The flip side is my inference, not a documented fact. Because one directory's contents live on one server, a single enormous busy directory is served by a single metadata server. Spreading files over many directories is the natural remedy, and the docs advise it anyway for very large directories. How is metadata stored? As extended attributes on a zero byte file in the local file system, one such file per user file. With large anodes, the attributes fit inside the anode itself, so one disk read finds everything. That's why the docs say to format X4 with 512 byte anodes, or 1024 if you stripe over more than four targets or use a CLs. A directory costs two directories and two metadata files, and a file costs one metadata file. Metadata grows linearly with the file count, and there's no central database to corrupt. The sizing rule of thumb, about .32.5% of total capacity, or roughly 150 million files per 500 gigabytes. The docs say X4 handles small file workloads significantly faster than other Linux file systems. But XFS allocates anodes dynamically, which helps if you're worried about running out. Compare the three. GPS spreads the work with a metanode per file in token managers. Luster scales metadata by adding targets and sharding directories. BGFS shards by directory from day one. Three different answers to the same bottleneck.
s6: What does BGFS promise when two clients touch the same file? This is where I have to be careful, because I could not find a clear statement of locking and consistency semantics in the documentation I read. The vendor says it's POSIX compatible. What the docs do describe is caching. Metadata is cached on the client only briefly by default. Milliseconds, controlled by three timeout settings. That means a stat on one client can return slightly old information about a change made on another. Data caching is its own setting. One client option chooses the file cache type and another controls syncing when a file closes. A third decides whether F-Sync commits to the server's disks or only to the server's cache. Switching that off cuts disk seeks and trades safety for speed. Version 8.4 adds an experimental feature, remote invalidation. The metadata server remembers which clients cached which in nodes and tells them when something changes. It's off by default and tracks up to 50 million in nodes, about 6 GB of server memory. The documentation is candid about the trade-offs. Changes can still become visible late. A race can lose an invalidation, leaving stale metadata for an unbounded, though self-healing time. Create heavy workloads see little benefit. And applications that use modification time or size as an instant signal shouldn't rely on it. My advice as a skeptic, if your application depends on cross-node locking or instant visibility, test it on your own system. The documentation I read doesn't settle the question.
s7: For the network, BGFS uses the open-fabrics verbs interface, so it supports InfiniBand, ROC, and Omnipath with RDMA and plain TCP otherwise. Management traffic still travels over TCP. Clients connect to metadata and storage servers. Metadata servers also connect to each other and to storage servers. Storage servers don't connect to other services. That's a tidy topology and it means you can count the connections. Here's the documented formula. Each node types maximum number of peers is for a metadata server the clients plus two times the other metadata servers plus the storage servers. For a storage server the clients plus the metadata servers. For a client metadata plus storage, a made-up example, a thousand clients, four metadata servers, and 20 storage servers gives up to a thousand 26 peers per metadata server and a thousand and four per storage server. Each connection has RDM buffers. By default 70 buffers of 8 kilobytes, about 560 kilobytes. The docs say the total should be at least one chunk and the default chunk is 512 which is presumably why. If each pair used one connection, my example works out to about 1.2 gigabytes of pinned memory permitted data server. The docs warn that RDM a memory can't be swapped out. Multi-rail has been available on the client since version 7.3. Point a configuration file at your IP over infinity band devices and traffic is balanced across them by connection count. Every interface must reach every service and they can't sit in separate subnets. A practical hazard, a misconfigured client can quietly fall back to TCP. The docs give a health command that shows which connections are RDM a so check it after setup.
s8: Now protection. BGFS protects data in two layers. Inside a target you use hardware RAID or ZFS as with the other systems. Across targets there's buddy mirroring. A buddy group is a pair of targets, a primary and a secondary. Data written to the primary is forwarded to the secondary. You pick targets of similar size on different servers or failure domains. Storage mirroring is set per directory and mirrored files take twice the space. Metadata can be mirrored too and once you enable it the root directory is mirrored by default. If a target drops out and comes back it usually re-sinks from its buddy automatically or you can start a re-sink by hand. Failover is an instant. The state change spreads to clients over time by default about 30 seconds and the docs say it should stay under a minute. During that window rights can be lost or a client can read stale data from the secondary. If a group is already degraded one more failure can lose data. An F-sink error on a secondary may go unnoticed until its next operation and mirroring is not a backup. It won't bring back a deleted or overwritten file. Here's the catch I promised. According to the vendors edition table mirroring high availability quota enforcement storage pools with tiering and several other features are enterprise only. The Community Edition is capped at 1000 terabytes of hard disk plus 200 of flash and beyond which will meet next is limited to five contributing nodes in both editions. So how BGFS compares with GPFS and Luster depends on which edition you mean. Check the table against your needs before assuming a feature is there.
s9: Now beyond spelled B E O N D short for B G F S on demand. It takes the local drives of the compute nodes allocated to a job and pools them into a temporary parallel file system for the length of the job. You start it with a list of hosts, a directory for raw data on each node, and a mount point. Every listed host becomes both a client and a server. The job end you stop it and optionally delete the data. It's usually wired into the schedulers prologue and epilogue scripts, with slurm and torque as the documented examples. Because it lives on local flash, it works as a burst buffer. The vendor says Fujitsu's Absai supercomputer uses it for a one petabyte, one terabyte per second in V M E burst buffer. That's a vendor claim relayed by the trade press, so treat it as indicative. Results should be staged out to persistent storage afterwards, and a parallel copy command helps. Now version eight, the biggest change in years. The management service was written from scratch in Rust with an SQL database. Management traffic moves to GRPC, which allows TLS encryption, and authentication moves to SH256. The old command line tool is replaced by a new one, written in Go, with noun verb commands, tables by default, and JSON output. The separate helper demon is gone. Version eight also adds remote storage targets, which link files and directories to S3 compatible object storage, with two new services to move data in parallel. Remote targets are an enterprise feature. One warning from the release notes. Version eight isn't compatible with older versions, because network and on-disc formats changed. Upgrades need a plan.
s10: Let's put all three side by side. Born, GPFS from IBM research in the early 1990s, Luster as a research project in 1999, and BGFS in 2005 at Fraunhofer. Metadata, GPFS spreads it across all nodes with tokens and a met node per file. Luster keeps it on metadata servers and shards with D and E. BGFS spreads directories across metadata servers from the start. Disk ownership, GPFS shares disks among nodes. Luster assigns each target to one server at a time. BGFS also keeps each target behind a storage service and mirrors across targets in pairs. Protection, GPFS has declustered raid in software or replication Luster relies on raid or ZFS under each target with mirrored layouts available. BGFS relies on raid or ZFS plus buddy mirroring in the enterprise edition. Consistency, GPFS documents single node equivalent semantics through tokens. Luster does it with a distributed lock manager. For BGFS, I couldn't verify the details from the documentation I read. That's the honest gap in this series and the first thing I'd test. A caution about the whole series. Three systems are not all of them. Others, such as WECCA, D-A-O-S, Cef-FS and Pan-FS, take different approaches and I haven't covered them. And no fair same hardware benchmark of these three came up in my research. So none of this tells you which is fastest. To recap BGFS, four services, chunk striping, set per directory, metadata sharded by directory, RDM and networking, buddy mirroring and many protection features in the paid edition, and beyond for job local file systems. The sources are on screen and the code is in the package.
